title: Grouping and Team Formation Problems
tagline: Year 3 — Dividing people into teams: together, apart and conditional rules; counting valid divisions

introduction.overview: A grouping puzzle divides a set of people into teams of equal size under rules such as "A and B are in the same team" or "C and D are in different teams". The teams are unordered, so a division such as {A,B,C} and {D,E,F} is the same as {D,E,F} and {A,B,C}. The method is to fix one person, apply the together and apart rules to build blocks, and then count the divisions that remain.
introduction.placementRelevance: Team-formation and grouping sets with six to eight people are a standard logical-reasoning pattern.
introduction.realWorldContext: Forming project groups, sports teams or lab pairs under compatibility rules is the same problem.

learningObjectives: Merge people who must be together into blocks
Use apart rules to separate blocks
Find people who are always or never together

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Dividing 6 people into two unordered teams of 3 can be done in C(6,3) ÷ 2 = 10 ways before conditions.

coreDefinitions: Unordered groups: swapping the names of two equal-sized groups gives the same division.
Together rule: the two people share a group, so treat them as one block.
Apart rule: the two people are in different groups.
Conditional rule: if two people are together, a third joins them.
Division: a complete split of everyone into groups.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A together rule glues people into a block; an apart rule keeps two blocks in different groups. After gluing and separating, few choices remain.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Fix the first person in group 1, glue the together pairs, place the apart pairs in opposite groups, then fill the remaining seats and count.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Block merge
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Count a glued pair as one person

mainNarrative: Six friends Asha, Bilal, Charu, Dev, Esha and Farid are split into two teams of 3. Asha and Bilal are in the same team; Charu and Dev are in different teams. Glue Asha and Bilal into a block of two; the third member of their team comes from Charu, Dev, Esha, Farid. If Charu joins, Dev must be in the other team, so the divisions are {Asha, Bilal, Charu} with {Dev, Esha, Farid}, and similarly for the others.

List the divisions by the third member of the Asha–Bilal team. A third member of Esha or Farid keeps Charu and Dev together in the other team, which breaks the apart rule. So only Charu or Dev can be the third member, and there are exactly two divisions.
Pairings use the same idea. For three pairs from six people, first pair the person with the most conditions, then pair the rest.
A person is "always with" another if in every valid division they share a group, and "never with" if they never share one. Check against the list.
For counts under a stated condition, filter the list of valid divisions by that condition.

deepDiveAspects.title: Unordered double-counting
deepDiveAspects.content: If you label the groups 1 and 2, every division is counted twice; divide by 2 for equal groups.

deepDiveAspects.title: Contradictory rules
deepDiveAspects.content: If a puzzle has zero valid divisions, a rule is misread; recheck the wording.

solvedExamples.title: Baseline count
solvedExamples.question: In how many ways can 6 people be divided into two unordered teams of 3 (no conditions)?

solvedExamples.title: Glue the pair
solvedExamples.question: Six people are divided into two teams of 3 with two of them (X and Y) always together. How many divisions are possible?

steps.title: Block
steps.explanation: X and Y form a team with one more of the other 4 people.

steps.title: Choices
steps.explanation: 4 ways to choose the third member.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The other team is then fixed.

solvedExamples.title: Apart rule
solvedExamples.question: Four people P, Q, R, S are divided into two teams of 2, with P and Q in different teams. How many divisions are possible?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Pair P with R or S.

steps.title: P's partner
steps.explanation: P can pair with R or S (not Q).

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Glue together pairs, separate apart pairs, fill the rest, count, and tick off against the list.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: List by the third member systematically.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating conditional rules as always true
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The rule fires only if the pair is together.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Apply it only in that case.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Reject options that put an apart pair together.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: List divisions by one person's teammates.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Lists stay short once together/apart rules are used.

easy.question:
Six friends 6 people (Asha, Bilal, Charu, Dev, Esha, Farid) are divided into groups of 3 (groups are not ordered). The following conditions apply:
1. Asha and Bilal are in the same group.
2. Charu and Dev are in different groups.

In how many ways can the people be divided?
easy.explanation: The valid divisions are {Asha, Bilal, Charu} and {Dev, Esha, Farid}; {Asha, Bilal, Dev} and {Charu, Esha, Farid}, so the number of ways is 2.

easy.explanation: The valid divisions are {Asha, Bilal, Charu} and {Dev, Esha, Farid}; {Asha, Bilal, Dev} and {Charu, Esha, Farid}; Bilal is with Asha in every valid division.
